extracted.intended_audience: EPA regulators, state environmental agencies, utilities (especially rural electric cooperatives), and regulatory/legal counsel
extracted.subtask_description: Legal/technical public comments arguing how EPA's proposed Clean Air Act §111(d) CO2 guidelines should be evaluated and revised — emphasizing state flexibility, consideration of facility-specific factors (remaining useful life, stranded investments), cost, and the achievability of BSER-based targets.

rubrics_metrics.name: Remaining useful life and other facility-specific considerations
rubrics_metrics.description: Remaining useful life and other facility-specific considerations should be taken into account in determining requirements directly applicable to affected EGUs and in setting state emission performance goals or compliance schedules.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EPA's proposal asserts these factors 'should not' affect state goals, but NRECA argues that states must be able to establish different glide paths/endpoints so facilities can continue economically through their remaining useful lives. Examples: single-EGU states (South Dakota), clusters of similarly aged units (LRS Wyoming), and recent major capital investments (Springerville Unit 3, Seminole). Statutory/regulatory support cited: 42 U.S.C. §§ 7411(a),(d); 40 C.F.R. §§ 60.22(b)(3),(5). Allowing consideration would avoid stranded investments and premature retirements; relief should include more relaxed standards or longer compliance periods for particular sources.

rubrics_metrics.name: State flexibility to set performance standards and compliance schedules
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA should limit itself to defining procedures and identifying the BSER; States must be permitted to determine the specific standards of performance to apply to sources within their borders, on a unit-by-unit basis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: NRECA urges EPA to adhere to the statute's command that states determine the extent to which to apply any standard of performance, using EPA procedures and BSER identification. The Proposed Rule's binding, statewide targets unlawfully deprive states of discretion, particularly needed for cooperatives and similarly situated utilities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Achievability requirement for a 'standard of performance' (BSER must be practically achievable)
rubrics_metrics.description: A 'standard of performance' must be achievable through application of the BSER; an infeasible or unattainable standard is not a valid standard of performance under the Clean Air Act.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If EPA prescribes BSER-generated savings assuming actions states cannot implement, the resulting target is invalid. The Proposed Rule is criticized as relying on a host of actions the States cannot themselves take, making targets unattainable and therefore arbitrary, capricious, and contrary to law (42 U.S.C. § 7411(a)(1)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Consideration of cost in determining BSER
rubrics_metrics.description: The 'cost of achieving such reduction' is a required statutory factor when determining the BSER and standards of performance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cites 42 U.S.C. § 7411(a) (specifying cost as a factor) and 40 C.F.R. § 60.22(b)(5) (emission guideline must reflect application of BSER 'considering the cost of such reduction'). EPA must account for costs, financing constraints, and rate impacts in setting guidelines and allowing state-level adjustments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirement for subcategorization where appropriate
rubrics_metrics.description: Emission guidelines must allow subcategorization — different emission guidelines or compliance times — when costs of control, physical limitations, geographical location, or similar factors make subcategorization appropriate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: 40 C.F.R. § 60.22(b)(5) requires subcategorization for different sizes, types, and classes of designated facilities when appropriate. NRECA argues the Proposed Rule's uniform statewide targets conflict with this requirement and ignore meaningful differences among units and utilities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Validation and adjustability of EPA assumptions (re-dispatch, renewables, demand reductions)
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA's assumptions about the availability of re-dispatch, renewable energy, and demand reduction must be validated and state goals must include mechanisms to reduce targets if those assumptions prove unfounded in particular cases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Proposed Rule bakes blanket assumptions into state targets without provision for adjustment. This unlawfully deprives states of the ability to address cooperatives' circumstances where re-dispatch/renewables/demand-side savings are unrealistic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consideration of financing arrangements and stranded asset/investment risks
rubrics_metrics.description: Standards and compliance schedules must account for existing financing arrangements and the risk of creating stranded assets or stranded investments which would have severe rate and economic impacts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Many cooperatives are highly leveraged with limited equity; modest reductions in operating hours may render units unable to service debt. Examples: Springerville Unit 3 (built 2006, invested ~$1B, useful life to 2066) and Seminole (>$530M invested in controls, much recent). EPA must permit state discretion to prevent premature uneconomic retirements and stranded investments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adequacy and flexibility of the state's 'toolbox' of emission reduction methods
rubrics_metrics.description: States' toolbox (gas, nuclear, renewables, energy efficiency) as proposed may be insufficient to address facility-specific issues; true offsets, alternate glide paths, and flexible timeframes should be available.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: NRECA argues the toolbox displaces generation rather than removes CO2 from atmosphere and therefore cannot, by itself, resolve concerns about remaining useful life and stranded investments. States should be able to use offsets and adopt more flexible compliance schedules to avoid severe economic consequences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirement that EPA provide procedures and cost information to States
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA must define the 'procedures' under which States will develop and submit plans and provide information on the costs of applying each system to designated facilities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Per 40 C.F.R. § 60.22(b)(3), EPA must provide cost information. NRECA asks EPA to confine itself to procedural definitions and BSER identification and leave source-specific standards to States using that information.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognition of regional/interregional grid complexity and limits on state jurisdiction
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA must account for the complexity of the electric power system (RTOs/ISOs, interconnections, economic dispatch, transmission constraints) and the limited scope of state authority over interstate transmission, wholesale markets, and certain resource choices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The comment explains diverse retail/wholesale structures (vertically integrated vs restructured states), ISO/RTO market operations, and physics of power flows. Because load is served by generation across state lines and contracts/engineering do not map simply to displaced units, EPA cannot assume states can reliably implement the redispatch/market-based changes the Proposed Rule presumes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consideration of cooperative-specific operational constraints (limited portfolios, heat-rate improvement limits, limited DSM opportunities)
rubrics_metrics.description: States should recognize that many rural electric cooperatives have small, coal-heavy portfolios, have already undertaken heat-rate improvements leaving little room for further gains, and have limited opportunities for demand-side energy efficiency improvements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: NRECA notes about 60% of cooperative baseload generation was built under the Fuel Use Act and is coal-based; heat-rate gains of 6% assumed by EPA may be unattainable for many units and tend to be temporary. Cooperative customer bases are predominantly residential, limiting DSM potential; therefore Building Blocks 1–4 assumptions may not apply to cooperatives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibition on EPA substituting its organizational/regulatory judgments for FERC/States
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA's rulemaking must not substitute EPA's judgment on the organization and regulation of the national electric generation/transmission system for that of FERC and the States.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Proposed Rule effectively imposes assumptions about dispatch, market structure, and resource choices at a national level; NRECA argues this intrudes upon areas governed by the Federal Power Act and state regulatory regimes and ignores the public-interest balancing inherent in state PUC decisions (IRPs, CPCNs, retail rate recovery).
